To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a novel flow immunocytochemical method has been developed for the quantitative and sensitive detection of lymphocytes undergoing in vitro and in vivo apoptosis.

a flow cytometric assay has been devised that allows the identification of apoptotically programmed cells in mixed populations of leukocytes and the immunophenotyping of the cells undergoing this process, and that the assay has been used to demonstrate that apoptotic lymphocyte death in vitro is a phenomenon related to disease progression in human immunodeficiencies and that apoptotic lymphoid cells can be detected in the circulating blood of a patient with advanced cancer after chemotherapy.

we have developed a quantitative flow immunocytochemical method for the detection and characterization of lymphocyte apoptosis in peripheral blood and that we have applied this assay to the analysis of the phenomenon of apoptosis in human immunodeficient patients.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel method for the detection and immunophenotypic characterization of apoptotic lymphoid cells in human peripheral blood and its application to the study of apoptosis in HIV infection and chemotherapy-induced lymphopenia.
the detection of lymphocytes undergoing the process of apoptosis in human immunodeficiencies.
the identification and characterization of the apoptotic cells generated in vitro and circulating in the periphery of patients with HIV infection and cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
apoptotic lymphocyte death in vivo is a phenomenon that occurs in a variety of clinical conditions.

apoptotic lymphoid cells are detectable in the circulation of patients with cancer, but not of patients with AIDS, and that the in vitro apoptosis observed in the cultures of lymphocytes from HIV patients is mostly due to the activation of CD8+ T lymphocytes.

apoptosis is a phenomenon of lymphocyte death occurring in vivo in patients treated with cytotoxic drugs, in patients with HIV infection and low CD4+ T cell counts, and in lymphocytes cultured in vitro from patients with HIV infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
apoptosis is a common phenomenon in the lymphocyte compartment and that it can be detected and quantitatively analyzed in the peripheral blood of cancer patients and of patients with AIDS.
the phenomenon of apoptosis can now be studied in vivo in patients, and that it might have a role in the pathogenesis of acquired immunodeficiency and cancer.
apoptosis is a common phenomenon of human lymphocytes, but it is not necessarily related to the pathogenesis of acquired immunodeficiency or of cytotoxic chemotherapy.
The main takeaway from our work is that

apoptosis is a common phenomenon that can be induced in vitro by several agents and can occur in vivo, as demonstrated by the identification of apoptosing lymphocytes in the peripheral blood of a patient with lymphoma shortly after high-dosage chemotherapy.
the phenomenon of in vivo lymphocyte apoptosis might be of relevance in the pathogenesis of acquired immunodeficiency disease syndrome.
the flow immunocytometry of apoptotic lymphocyte subpopulations is a sensitive and quantitative method for their detection in vivo and in vitro.
